source.title: Gradient flow in the gaussian covariate model: exact solution of learning curves and multiple descent structures

record.tranche_reason: The study analytically and experimentally examines descent curves using Gaussian-covariate, linear, random-feature, kernel, and realistic-dataset settings rather than reproducing the original deep-network experiments.
record.gate_note: The introduction and references cite earlier double-descent results, but those cited results are not rows. Rows below record this study’s own results.
record.test_reason: The study derives exact gradient-flow test-error curves in a Gaussian covariate model and checks them against MNIST and Fashion-MNIST. Its own results show sample-ratio peaks, multiple descents and epoch-wise descents, which bear on V2, V3, V4 and V6. It does not reproduce the deep-network experiments, so it is T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors claim a unified asymptotic framework giving the full gradient-flow time evolution of training and test error in the Gaussian covariate model. It recovers known double descents, constructs any number of descents in φ and in time, and matches MNIST/Fashion-MNIST gradient-descent curves, with slight upward bias near the peak. The noted mismatches come from the appendix; the formal conclusion only discusses DMFT and polynomial-scaling extensions.
record.recipe_differences: The original claim concerns deep-network experiments. This study uses asymptotic Gaussian-covariate theory, linear/ridgeless regression and related model classes, gradient flow, and experiments on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST.
record.method_sensitivity: The number and timing of peaks depend on the non-isotropic subspace scaling parameter α and the sample-to-dimension ratio φ. The MNIST discussion reports mismatch around the peak and says the mismatch is more pronounced for smaller λ.

fits_no_version.finding: Each new peak coincides with the emergence of a new bulk in the student data's eigenvalue distribution. Multiple bulks give multiple time scales, and hence multiple epoch-wise peaks (Figures 3 and 6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The number and timing of descent peaks are set by the number and spacing of spectral bulks in the input covariance.

record.problems: The main multiple-descent results are theoretical and rely on high-dimensional assumptions. Several plotted outcomes are not numerically tabulated. Realistic-dataset experiments use 10 or 20 runs, and the authors report deviations around the double-descent peak and as n approaches ntot.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results were left out. Related results cited in the introduction and bibliography were excluded because they are not this study’s own findings.

untested.parts: All of it: no deep networks or model-size sweeps of deep nets.
Deep networks; epoch-wise shape on real data is not described.
Whether optimally tuned regularization removes the peak; only very small λ values are used.

missing.what: Fashion-MNIST least-squares learning profile over n and time evolution at n=700. Test error is slightly above prediction for n<10^3, and the mismatch grows at lower λ, which increases the double-descent effect.
Mismatched ridgeless regression closed form (eq. 175): error diverges at κ=φ0/γ=1, including through a misspecification term (1−γ)r², even when σ=0.
MNIST mismatch around the peak is more pronounced for smaller λ; this is a qualitative λ dependence of the peak.

record.verdict_notes: All main results are non-rigorous asymptotics (concentration assumptions; λ=0 assumed valid). The anisotropic multiple-descent model is noiseless, so its peaks come from input-scale structure rather than label noise. This is consistent with the 'or variance' wording of V6 but not with a label-noise-only reading. R7 was downgraded to cannot_determine because the epoch-wise shape on MNIST is never described.

versions.untested_parts: Deep-network test error as a function of model size; the study does not test deep networks.
The epoch-wise behavior is studied in specified Gaussian-covariate and dataset settings, not across deep networks generally.
The sample-size effect is shown for ridgeless linear regression and MNIST; it is not tested across deep-network settings generally.
The results concern the model classes and regimes studied here, not every model class or a general risk theorem.
The study does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across size, epochs, and sample size.

The study demonstrates multiple descents, including epoch-wise descents, in particular settings. It does not test whether label noise or variance drives the peaks, or whether optimally tuned regularization makes them disappear.
The study does not test whether counting complexity by an effective number of parameters turns second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: ridgeless regression of a noisy linear function
rows.size_stated: p and n grow with fixed ratios
rows.operation_detail: Derived the minimum least-squares test error as a function of the sample-to-feature ratio φ0.
rows.value: Egen(+∞) = 0 for ζ = 0; Egen(+∞) = σ²φ0/(φ0−1) for ζ = 1−φ0 when φ0 > 1; Egen(+∞) = r²(1−φ0) + σ²φ0/(1−φ0) for ζ = 1−φ0 when φ0 < 1.
rows.note: The piecewise formula gives a divergent test-error term on approach to the interpolation ratio from either side when σ is nonzero.
rows.check: The value's case labels look garbled. In the text, ζ=0 gives σ²φ0/(φ0−1) (φ0>1), and ζ=1−φ0 gives the φ0<1 branch. The divergence comes only from the σ² term, so with σ=0 there is no peak; this bears on V6's noise part. The result re-derives Hastie et al./Belkin et al. inside the study's own framework.

source_check.correct: Egen(+∞)=σ²φ0/(φ0−1) for ζ=0, φ0>1; Egen(+∞)=r²(1−φ0)+σ²/(1−φ0) for ζ=1−φ0, φ0<1. Divergence at φ0=1 requires σ>0.
source_check.problem: The recorded piecewise formula incorrectly assigns zero error to ζ=0 and misassigns the noisy φ0>1 branch.
